Learning objectives

Add links to external websites and other course pages.
Insert an image and provide alternative text.
Embed a video in a content page.

Remember accessibility

Use the training content pages to provide learning materials and activities for your participants.
You can organise the pages to suit the structure of your training (for example: by day, module, topic, or section) or structure them around what participants need to learn and do.
In this template, the pages demonstrate how to use Markdown and Quarto to organise and format content. They are examples to adapt when building your own training pages. Replace the example material with your own, and remove any examples or sections you do not need.
The template pages cover:

Module 1 – How to structure a page: Headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, code blocks, and text formatting.
Module 2 – How to highlight information: Callouts for tips, notes, important information, and warnings, as well as reflection questions.
Module 3 – How to add media and interactive elements: Links, images, videos, and exercises.

FAQ
A well-organised page helps participants find information and understand how ideas relate to one another. In addition to headings and lists, Quarto supports elements such as block quotes, tables, and horizontal rules.
This page demonstrates a few ways to structure information. Copy the examples and adapt them to your own course.

title: Ways to organise content
text:
Block quotes
Use a block quote to set apart a quotation or a statement from another source.

Clear structure helps readers navigate information and focus on the main message.

Markdown syntax:
> Clear structure helps readers navigate information and focus on the main message.

title: Ways to organise content
text:
Tables
Tables are useful for presenting information that is easier to compare in rows and columns. Keep them concise and use clear column headings.



Element
Purpose
Example




Heading
Introduces a section
Learning objectives


Paragraph
Explains an idea
A short description


List
Groups related items
Steps or key points



Markdown syntax:
| Element | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Heading | Introduces a section | Learning objectives |
| Paragraph | Explains an idea | A short description |
| List | Groups related items | Steps or key points |

title: Ways to organise content
text:
Horizontal rules
A horizontal rule can separate distinct parts of a page. Use it sparingly, when a visual break helps clarify the structure.

Markdown syntax:
---

title: Ways to organise content
text:
Combining organisational elements
You can combine headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, and other elements on the same page. Choose the format that makes the information easiest to follow.
For example, a section describing a course activity could include a short introduction followed by a table of practical details.
Example Markdown:
## Course activity

In this activity, participants will work in small groups to discuss the topic.

| Detail | Description |
|---|---|
| Format | Group discussion |
| Duration | 20 minutes |
| Materials | Discussion questions |

### Instructions

1. Form a small group.
2. Read the discussion questions.
3. Share your ideas with the group.
4. Summarise the main points.

title: Structuring a page
text:
Overview
Content
Schedule

Information

Preparation
Practicalities
Announcements
Resources
Team
Syllabus
FAQ
A well-structured page helps participants follow the learning material and find information easily. You can use headings, paragraphs, lists, and text formatting to organise your content.
This page demonstrates some of the most common elements you may want to use when creating course materials. Each example includes a code snippet that you can copy and adapt.

title: Structuring a page
text:
Add headings
Headings divide a page into sections and make the content easier to navigate. They also appear in the table of contents on the right-hand side of the page.
Use two hash symbols (##) for a main section heading and three (###) for a subsection.
For example, this code:
## Main section

Text introducing the section.

### Subsection

More detailed information.
produces a main section heading followed by a smaller subsection heading.
Use headings in a logical order. Avoid choosing a heading level only because you prefer its appearance.

title: Structuring a page
text:
Add paragraphs
Write ordinary text as paragraphs. Leave a blank line between paragraphs to make them separate.
For example:
This is the first paragraph. Use it to introduce a topic
or explain an idea.

This is the second paragraph. It appears separately from
the first paragraph.
You can write paragraphs directly in your .qmd file without adding any special formatting.

title: Structuring a page
text:
Format text
You can use bold or italic text to emphasise important words or phrases.
Bold text is useful for key terms or important information.
Italic text can be used for emphasis or to introduce a term.
Copy these examples:
This is **bold text**.

This is *italic text*.

You can also combine them: ***bold and italic text***.
Use text formatting sparingly so that it remains meaningful to readers.

title: Structuring a page
text:
Create a bulleted list
Use a hyphen (-) at the beginning of each line to create a bulleted list.
For example:
- First item
- Second item
- Third item
This is useful when presenting related points that do not need to be followed in a particular order.

Create a nested list
You can indent items to create a list within a list:
- Main item
  - Supporting point
  - Another supporting point
- Another main item

title: Structuring a page
text:
Numbered steps
Use a numbered list when the order of the items matters, such as for instructions or a process.

Open the course page.
Find the section you want to update.
Replace the example text with your own content.
Render the website and review the result.

Markdown syntax
1. Open the course page.
2. Find the section you want to update.
3. Replace the example text with your own content.
4. Render the website and review the result.

title: Structuring a page
text:
Add learning objectives
Learning objectives can help participants understand what they should be able to do after completing a topic.
You can introduce them with a short paragraph followed by a bulleted list.
For example:
After completing this module/topic/etc, you will be able to:

Describe the main concept.
Explain why it is relevant.
Apply the concept in a practical situation.

Copy and replace the example objectives with your own:
**After completing this module/topic/etc, you will be able to:**

- [Add learning objective 1]
- [Add learning objective 2]
- [Add learning objective 3]

title: Structuring a page
text:
Combine different elements
You can combine headings, paragraphs, and lists to build a complete topic page.
Here is a simple structure you can use as a starting point:
## Introduction

Introduce the topic and explain why it is relevant.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this topic, you should be able to:

- [Add learning objective 1]
- [Add learning objective 2]
- [Add learning objective 3]

## Main content

Explain the main ideas.

### First concept

Add information about the first concept.

### Second concept

Add information about the second concept.

## Summary

Summarise the key points from the topic.
You do not need to use every section. Adapt the structure to suit your learning material.






Tip



Start with a clear page structure before adding detailed content. A few meaningful headings and short paragraphs can make a long topic much easier to read.

title: Putting it together
text:
The source Markdown
The example above can be created using the following Quarto Markdown structure. Copy it into a .qmd file and adapt the content.
## Example: Introducing a course topic

### Overview

In this section, introduce the topic and explain why it is relevant to participants.

Clear introductory text helps participants understand what they will learn and how the topic connects to the course.

### Learning objectives

By the end of this section, participants will be able to:

- Describe the main concept introduced in the section.
- Identify key information related to the topic.
- Apply the concept in a practical context.

### Key information

| Topic element | Example content |
|---|---|
| Main concept | Introduce the central idea |
| Key information | Explain the most important points |
| Practical application | Show how the concept can be used |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Tip

Use callouts to highlight information that participants should notice. Keep the message focused, and avoid using callouts for information that belongs in the main text.
:::

### Activity

Give participants an opportunity to apply what they have learned.

**Instructions**

1. Read the example or scenario.
2. Discuss the questions with a partner or group.
3. Identify the main points from the discussion.
4. Share your conclusions.

### Reflection

Ask participants to consider how the topic relates to their own work or experience.

- What is one important idea you learned?
- How could you apply it in your own context?
- What would you like to explore further?
